title: Serving Runtime: Architecture, Scheduling, Profiling, Benchmarking & Runbooks
author: Liam Chen
content:
Overview

Purpose:
This document is the canonical serving runtime reference for the inference team. It consolidates the runtime architecture, kernel scheduling policies, profiling playbooks, benchmarking suite, recent release notes, known issues, operational runbooks, and links to the team wiki. It is intended for engineers, SREs, and incident responders.

Scope:
- Hosted, Dedicated and Private runtime deployments
- GPU-optimized inference path (CUDA + Triton-like worker)
- Scheduler and continuous-batching logic
- Profiling and benchmark procedures used for releases and performance regressions

1) Runtime architecture (high level)

Components and service names:
- inference-gateway: HTTP/GRPC front door (auth, rate limit, routing)
- request-router: routes by policy (latency/cost/region/customer-tier)
- scheduler: implements batching, kernel selection, and queueing policies (service name: runtime-scheduler)
- model-manager: model lifecycle, versioning, quantization profiles (service name: model-store)
- gpu-worker: per-GPU worker process running the inference engine (process: rw-worker)
- kv-cache: prefix and KV cache for past tokens (service name: kv-cache)
- telemetry-collector: metrics/traces exporter (service name: telemetry-ingest)

Data flow (text description):
1. inference-gateway authenticates request, enriches with customer config and route policy.
2. request-router maps request to a model variant and target pool. If cached prefixes exist in kv-cache, a cache hit short-circuits token generation.
3. scheduler evaluates queuing/batching policy and assigns request to a gpu-worker.
4. gpu-worker executes model kernels, updates KV cache and returns streaming tokens to gateway.
5. telemetry-collector emits metrics and traces for latency, GPU utilization, kernel timings and cache hit rates.

Design notes and tradeoffs:
- Single-process per GPU worker for predictable memory usage and simpler CUDA context management.
- Scheduler maintains soft reservations for latency-sensitive customers to reduce tail latency.
- Continuous batching favors throughput but will cap batch sizes to meet p95/p99 latency SLOs.

2) Kernel scheduling and execution strategy

Goals:
- Meet latency SLOs (p95/p99) for latency-tier customers while maximizing token/sec for batch workloads.
- Avoid GPU OOMs and excessive context switching.

Policy overview:
- Priority classes: REALTIME > IMPORTANT > BEST_EFFORT. Each class has a max_batch_size and preemption policy.
- Per-GPU reservation: a portion of GPU SMs are logically reserved (via stream priority and CUDA Graph warm paths) for REALTIME workloads during high load.
- Continuous batching window: default 8ms (configurable per pool).
- Batch size caps: default per-model caps (see Benchmark Matrix) and global max 1024 tokens per batch.
- Preemption: we use cooperative preemption at request boundaries; long-running large batches can be split if a REALTIME request arrives.

Key config knobs (table):
- scheduler.batch_window_ms: "8"
- scheduler.max_batch_tokens: "1024"
- scheduler.realtime_reserved_fraction: "0.15"  # fraction of capacity reserved for REALTIME
- scheduler.priority_classes: "REALTIME,IMPORTANT,BEST_EFFORT"
- worker.cuda_streams_per_model: "2"
- worker.cuda_graph_warmup: "true"

Kernel selection and tuning:
- Model kernel profiles are generated during onboarding (see quantization-profiles). The model-manager stores preferred kernel variants by sequence length and batch size.
- Runtime picks kernel variant based on (model, seq_len, batch_tokens) using a precomputed cost model.

3) Profiling playbook (step-by-step)

When to profile:
- New model onboarding
- Performance regression detected in benchmarking or prod
- Investigating high p99 latency incidents

Tools used:
- nsys (NVIDIA Nsight Systems) for end-to-end GPU+CPU traces
- nvprof (deprecated) only for legacy nodes
- nvidia-smi for quick GPU stats
- perf / bpftrace for kernel-level CPU sampling
- py-spy for Python sampling in worker processes
- custom trace exporter: telemetry-ingest captures LTTng-style span metadata

Quick trace collection (recommended):
1. Identify node and pid: ps aux | grep rw-worker
2. Collect lightweight timeline: sudo nsys profile --capture-range=none -o /tmp/trace --trace=cuda,osrt -t 10 --force-track-launch --attach-pid <PID>
3. For full kernel timings (when reproducing locally): sudo nsys profile -o /tmp/fulltrace --trace=cuda,osrt,syscalls -t 60 --capture-range=per-profiler --attach-pid <PID>
4. Export summary: nsys stats /tmp/fulltrace.qdrep --report=summary
5. Capture python sampling: sudo py-spy record -o /tmp/pyspy.svg --pid <PID> --duration 30

Profiling checklist:
- Confirm environment: CUDA_DRIVER >= 525, nsys >= 2023.3
- Reproduce small, medium, and large sequence-length cases (e.g., 32, 256, 2048 tokens).
- Capture both cold-start and warm-path (with KV cache hit) traces.
- Record GPU temperatures, clock throttles and ECC errors (nvidia-smi -q).

Common profiling patterns and fixes:
- Excessive memcpy H2D/D2H: enable pinned memory and prefetch host-to-device for inputs.
- Kernel launch serialization: increase CUDA streams per model to 2 and enable concurrent kernel launch.
- Suboptimal kernel choice: update model-store kernel profiles and re-run kernel selector training.

4) Benchmarking suite and standard tests

Repo and harness:
- Repository: git.redwood/confluence/eng-serving-runtime/benchmarks (internal)
- Runner: bench-runner service (bench-runner CLI)
- CI integration: nightly benchmarks against canary cluster and full weekly matrix

Standard Benchmark Matrix (text):
- Models: small (Llama-7B-8k), medium (Llama-13B-32k), large (Redwood-70B-64k-fp16)
- Sequence lengths: 32, 256, 1024, 2048, 4096, 8192
- Batch sizes (requests): 1, 4, 8, 16
- Metrics captured: p50/p95/p99 latency (ms), tokens/sec, GPU util (%), GPU mem (MiB), CPU util (%), cache_hit_rate (%)

Sample bench config (JSON example):
{
  "model": "llama-13b-32k",
  "seq_len": "1024",
  "batch_size": "8",
  "num_iters": "500",
  "warmup_iters": "50",
  "metric_exporter": "prometheus"
}

Baseline targets (lab cluster, 8x A100-80GB):
- Llama-7B-8k @ batch=8, seq=256: p95 < 120ms, tokens/sec > 75k
- Llama-13B-32k @ batch=4, seq=1024: p95 < 220ms, tokens/sec > 30k
- Redwood-70B @ batch=1, seq=2048: p95 < 500ms, tokens/sec > 6k

Benchmark automation:
- Nightly: small models + quick matrix (smoke)
- Weekly: full matrix against staging cluster
- Before release: run full benchmark suite and attach report to release notes

5) Release notes (recent entries)

- v3.4.0 (2026-01-15) - Improvement
  - Scheduler: reduced batch_window_ms default from 12ms -> 8ms improving p95 by ~18% for small models.
  - Kernel cache: introduced kernel-variant caching mechanism reducing kernel selection overhead by 10-20%.
  - Bugfix: fixed memory leak in kv-cache for prefix evictions.

- v3.3.2 (2025-11-02) - Patch
  - Fix: GPU worker would occasionally deadlock when CUDA graph warmup failed; fallback path added.
  - Fix: improved telemetry for batch composition (adds per-request batch ids).

Release checklist (required for all runtime releases):
1. Run full benchmark matrix and attach report.
2. Validate profiling traces for representative models.
3. Run canary rollout (5% traffic) for 24 hours and monitor p99 latency and error budget.
4. Run integration tests: auth, rate-limits, model fallback, KV cache behavior.
5. Update release notes and changelog.

6) Known issues (current)

- ISSUE-2026-014: Large-sequence OOM when batch_tokens > 2048 on older GPU types (P4/P40). Severity: High. Workaround: enforce model-specific max_batch_tokens in scheduler or move traffic to A100/A800 nodes. Owner: eng-infra.
- ISSUE-2026-021: Occasional p99 spikes on MIXED workloads with heavy KV cache churn. Severity: Medium. Workaround: increase realtime_reserved_fraction to 0.25 for impacted pools. Owner: serving-runtime.
- ISSUE-2025-198: nvprof-based diagnostics failing on upgraded nodes (driver mismatch). Severity: Low. Workaround: use nsys or repro on legacy nodes. Owner: tools-team.

7) Runbooks (operational procedures)

Runbook A: High p99 latency for a model route
1. Identify affected route: metrics -> per-route p99 > SLO (default p99 SLO = "500ms" for standard tier; realtime tier = "150ms").
2. Check recent releases and canary: if recent runtime release in last 24h, roll back canary using console (route -> rollout -> rollback).
3. Check scheduler metrics: scheduler.queue_length, scheduler.batch_window_ms, scheduler.batch_tokens_histogram.
4. If queueing high and batch_token sizes large: reduce scheduler.batch_window_ms to 4ms for the pool and monitor.
5. If GPU saturation (gpu_util > 95%): scale up pool (add nodes) or reduce batch size cap for BEST_EFFORT classes.
6. Escalate to serving-runtime oncall if changes do not reduce p99 within 15 minutes.

Runbook B: GPU OOM on worker
1. Identify OOM logs: worker logs show CUDA OOM and stack traces.
2. Immediately evict BEST_EFFORT queues on the node: curl -X POST http://runtime-scheduler/admin/evict?node=<node-id>&class=BEST_EFFORT
3. Restart rw-worker process: sudo systemctl restart rw-worker and tail logs.
4. If OOM persists after restart, copy /var/log/rw-worker/*.log and create incident with priority P1.
5. Possible mitigations: enable model quantization profile, reduce max_batch_tokens, move models to larger GPUs.

Runbook C: GPU node failure (hardware)
1. Mark node as unschedulable in cluster: kubectl cordon <node>.
2. Drain running workers and migrate hot models: kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data.
3. Notify eng-infra to open a hardware ticket and to replace the node.
4. Rebalance reserved REALTIME capacity by temporarily increasing reserved_fraction on other nodes.

Appendix: Config snippets and commands

Example scheduler config (YAML):
scheduler:
  batch_window_ms: 8
  max_batch_tokens: 1024
  realtime_reserved_fraction: 0.15
  priority_classes: [REALTIME, IMPORTANT, BEST_EFFORT]

Quick diagnostics commands:
- Check per-route p99: curl -s http://telemetry-ingest/metrics | grep route:my-route | grep p99
- Check GPU stats: nvidia-smi --query-gpu=utilization.gpu,memory.used,temperature.gpu --format=csv
- Tail worker logs: sudo journalctl -u rw-worker -f --since "10 minutes ago"

Ownership and SLAs
- Serving Runtime team: primary owner for runtime-scheduler, gpu-worker, kv-cache.
- SRE/Eng Infra: owner for scaling, cluster, GPU provisioning.
- Product: defines customer tier SLOs and pricing impacts.

SLO summary (examples):
- Realtime tier: p95 < 120ms, p99 < 250ms, error_rate < 0.1%
- Standard tier: p95 < 300ms, p99 < 500ms, error_rate < 0.5%
- Throughput: baseline tokens/sec targets are maintained by nightly benchmarks and attached to release notes.

Contact and governance
- For proposed changes to kernel scheduling or scheduler defaults, open an ADR in /confluence/architecture-and-standards/decision-records and tag reviewers from eng-serving-runtime and eng-sre.

Document maintenance
- Owner: Liam Chen (serving-runtime)
- Review cadence: quarterly. Update this doc after each major release and after incident postmortems affecting scheduler or kernel choices.

Related artifacts:
- Runtime profiling templates: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/profiling-templates
- Benchmark reports: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/benchmarks/reports/ (archived per-run)

End of document.
